overview:
Uvasaggaharam Stotra (often also called Uvasaggaharam Sutra) is a revered Jain hymn dedicated to the twenty‑third Tirthankara, Lord Parshvanatha. It is composed in Prakrit and is traditionally attributed to Acharya Bhadrabahu, a prominent Jain teacher dated in popular accounts to around the 4th–3rd century BCE. Within Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka practice it is counted among the Nav Smaran, the nine sacred hymns frequently recited for remembrance, devotion, and protection. The stotra focuses on Parshvanatha as the remover of obstacles (upsarga), the destroyer of poisonous defilements, and the abode of auspiciousness and well‑being.

The core text is usually transmitted as a compact five‑verse hymn, though some traditions and pedagogical editions append additional verses that praise Bhadrabahu or elaborate the benefits of devotion to Parshvanatha. The language is a devotional Prakrit, with strong emphasis on karmic purification, removal of planetary afflictions, disease, and suffering, and the attainment of right faith (samyaktva) and ultimately liberation (mokṣa). The hymn repeatedly describes Parshvanatha as "kammaghaṇa‑mukkaṃ"—free from the dense mass of karma—and as the one who destroys "visa" (poison), both in the literal sense of harmful substances and in the metaphorical sense of inner defilements.

In lived practice, Uvasaggaharam Stotra is recited by lay Jains and sometimes by monastics during times of difficulty, illness, travel, or perceived astrological or environmental danger. The second verse refers to the "visahara‑phulliṃga mantra"—a charm or mantra that, when held at the neck (symbolically remembered and recited), is said to calm evil planetary effects, disease, epidemics, and the pains of old age. The text then emphasizes that even setting aside the specific mantra, sincere bowing to Parshvanatha itself yields great fruits, protecting beings from misery and misfortune.

The stotra also has a strong soteriological dimension. Later verses compare the attainment of right faith in Parshvanatha to obtaining wish‑fulfilling jewels (cintāmaṇi) and wish‑fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), yet declare that true faith is superior to these worldly boons. Through unimpeded devotion and correct understanding, beings are said to reach the "ayarāmaraṃ ṭhāṇaṃ"—the ageless, deathless state of liberation. The final verse is a personal prayer: the devotee, with a heart full of bhakti, praises the "mahāyasa" (greatly glorious) Parshvanatha and asks to be granted bodhi—right perception and knowledge—in every birth.

Across Jain communities, Uvasaggaharam Stotra is widely respected. Śvetāmbara sources explicitly list it among the Nav Smaran, and Digambara traditions also preserve and recite the hymn, though there may be minor textual variants in manuscripts and regional recensions. Scholarly and community explanations stress that its primary function is to orient the mind toward the Jina, cultivate trust in the protective power of right faith, and remind practitioners that true protection lies in ethical conduct and spiritual progress rather than in mere ritual or magical expectation.

primary_sources.title: Uvasaggaharam Stotra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Acharya Bhadrabahu
primary_sources.original_text:
उवसग्गहरं पासं, पासं वंदामि कम्मघण-मुक्कं ।
विसहर-विस-णिण्णासं मंगल कल्लाण आवासं ॥
विसहर-फुल्लिंगमंतं कंठे धारेइ जो सया मणुओ ।
तस्स गह-रोग-मारी, दुट्ठ-जरा जंति उवसामं ॥
चिट्ठउ दूरे मंतो, तुज्झ पणामो वि बहुफलो होइ ।
नर तिरिएसु वि जीवा, पावंति न दुक्ख-दोगच्चं ॥
तुह सम्मत्ते लद्धे चिंतामणि कप्प-पायव-ब्भहिए ।
पावंति अविग्घेणं जीवा अयरामरं ठाणं ॥
इह संथुओ महायस भत्ति-भर-निब्भरेण हिअएण ।
ता देव! दिज्ज बोहिं, भवे भवे पास जिणचंद ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
uvasaggaharaṃ pāsaṃ, pāsaṃ vaṃdāmi kammaghaṇa-mukkaṃ .
visahara-visa-ninnāsaṃ maṃgala-kallāṇa-āvāsaṃ ..
visahara-phulliṃga-maṃtaṃ kaṃṭhe dhārei jo sayā maṇuo .
tassa gaha-roga-mārī, duṭṭha-jarā jaṃti uvasāmaṃ ..
ciṭṭhaü dūre maṃto, tujjha paṇāmo vi bahuphalo hoi .
nara tiriesu vi jīvā, pāvaṃti na dukkha-dogaccaṃ ..
tuha sammatte laddhe ciṃtāmaṇi kappa-pāyava-bbhahie .
pāvaṃti aviggheṇaṃ jīvā ayarāmaraṃ ṭhāṇaṃ ..
iha saṃthuo mahāyasa bhatti-bhara-nibbhareṇa hiaeṇa .
tā deva! dijja bohiṃ, bhave bhave pāsa jiṇacaṃda ..
primary_sources.translation:
I bow to Lord Parshvanath, who is attended by the distress‑removing Parshwa deity, who is free from all types of karma, who is the destroyer of poisonous defilements, and who is the abode of auspiciousness and well‑being.

If one always holds at his neck the charm of the visahara‑phulliṃga mantra, his evil planetary effects, diseases, epidemics, and the pains of wicked old age are calmed down.

Let aside that mantra; even your mere salutation yields abundant fruits. Humans and beings in the animal realms who bow to you do not fall into misery and wretchedness.

By attaining right faith in you, which is like obtaining the wish‑fulfilling jewel and the wish‑fulfilling tree, beings, without any hindrance, reach the ageless, immortal state.

Here, with a heart filled with devotion, you are praised, O greatly glorious one. O Lord, O Parshva Jina‑chandra, grant me enlightenment (bodhi, the three jewels) in every birth.
primary_sources.notes: This text is preserved in Prakrit and appears in Śvetāmbara collections of stotras, where it is listed among the Nav Smaran (nine sacred hymns). The attribution to Acharya Bhadrabahu is traditional and widely repeated in community literature, though exact historical verification of authorship and date is difficult. Different manuscripts and sectarian recensions show minor variations in wording—such as small changes in compounds or verb forms—but the core five‑verse structure and devotional meaning remain stable. Later pedagogical editions sometimes append verses praising Bhadrabahu or elaborating the benefits of serving Parshvanatha, yet these are understood as expansions rather than part of the earliest core hymn.

misconceptions.myth: Uvasaggaharam Stotra works as a guaranteed magical charm that automatically removes all worldly problems regardless of conduct.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional explanations emphasize that the stotra’s protective power is linked to right faith, ethical living, and sincere devotion to Parshvanatha. While the text speaks of calming planetary afflictions, disease, and suffering, Jain doctrine holds that karmic results are shaped by one’s own actions and inner transformation, not by mechanical recitation alone. The hymn is meant to orient the mind toward the Jina and support spiritual progress, not to replace responsible action, medical care, or moral effort.

misconceptions.myth: The stotra belongs exclusively to one Jain sect and is not respected or used outside that tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Uvasaggaharam Stotra is prominently preserved and classified among the Nav Smaran in Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka practice, but it is also known and recited in other Jain communities, including Digambara traditions, with minor textual variants. The core praise of Parshvanatha as remover of obstacles and giver of auspiciousness is shared across sectarian lines, even though specific liturgical settings and manuscript readings may differ.

misconceptions.myth: Every printed version of Uvasaggaharam Stotra represents a single, fixed original text without any variation or historical development.
misconceptions.reality: Manuscript evidence and community publications show small differences in wording, spelling, and verse count between editions. Some sources present four core verses, others five, and still others add additional verses praising Bhadrabahu or elaborating the benefits of serving Parshvanatha. These variations are typical of pre‑modern transmission and do not fundamentally alter the devotional or doctrinal meaning of the hymn, but they remind readers that the text has a living history rather than a single frozen form.
